context.title: Working in Shenzhen: Discussion Context
body: A Hong Kong graduate has accepted an entry-level finance job in Shenzhen after finding few suitable openings at home. His salary is similar to what he expected in Hong Kong, while rent and daily expenses are lower. He also believes that working in a fast-growing business district will give him experience with new markets and clients.

The move has not been effortless. His journey to work is long, office practices are unfamiliar, and some websites and online services he normally uses are unavailable. Although he can return to Hong Kong at weekends, he misses his family and established circle of friends. He advises applicants to compare the whole employment package instead of focusing only on salary.

More Hongkongers may consider cross-border work as transport links improve and companies expand in the Greater Bay Area. However, a decision should also take account of language, workplace culture, housing, career development and personal responsibilities. Anyone interested should visit the city, speak to current employees and agree clear employment terms before accepting an offer.

context.title: Giving money to parents: Discussion Context
body: In some Hong Kong families, adult children regularly give part of their income to their parents. The payment may help with household bills, medical expenses or retirement, but it can also be a symbolic way of expressing gratitude. Parents who supported their children for many years may value the gesture even when they do not depend on the money.

The custom can become difficult when young adults are paying rent, saving for a home or caring for children of their own. A fixed amount that seems reasonable in one household may create pressure in another. Problems are more likely when expectations are never discussed or when brothers and sisters contribute very different amounts.

Families could treat financial support as one possible form of care rather than a compulsory test of respect. Time, practical help, regular contact and support at medical appointments may be equally meaningful. An honest conversation about needs and affordability can help parents and children find an arrangement that protects both family relationships and financial security.

context.title: Hong Kong Book Fair: Discussion Context
body: The Hong Kong Book Fair attracts large crowds because visitors can browse many publishers in one place, meet writers and discover books at promotional prices. A central theme can give the event a clearer identity. One recent fair highlighted Chinese martial arts literature, including novels, manuscripts, comics and screen adaptations connected with well-known Hong Kong writers.

Supporters said the theme introduced younger readers to an influential part of popular culture and showed overseas visitors how local stories had travelled across languages and media. Others felt that a single genre could not represent the variety of books published in Hong Kong, and that crowded sales booths sometimes received more attention than reading itself.

A future theme should be broad enough to include different ages, languages and types of writing. Possible choices include stories of Hong Kong neighbourhoods, science and the future, or books that became films. Exhibitions, talks and workshops could then turn the fair into a cultural experience rather than only a large marketplace.

context.title: Cantonese: Discussion Context
body: People who settle in Hong Kong without speaking Cantonese can often manage at international workplaces, yet everyday situations may still be difficult. Talking to taxi drivers, understanding notices in small shops and joining conversations with neighbours can require local language skills. These barriers may leave newcomers dependent on friends or separated from parts of community life.

Learning Cantonese can make practical tasks easier and help people understand humour, television, food culture and local concerns. It may also widen employment choices and make friendships with Cantonese-speaking residents more natural. Progress can be slow because pronunciation and tones are unfamiliar, while many courses do not fit adults’ working hours.

Language classes are only one solution. Schools, employers and community groups could organise conversation partners, subtitled activities and neighbourhood visits where learners use simple Cantonese without embarrassment. Local speakers can help by being patient and avoiding switching languages immediately. Connection should be a shared effort rather than a test newcomers must pass alone.

context.title: Ice Bucket Challenge: Discussion Context
body: The Ice Bucket Challenge spread rapidly because it combined a simple action, a public nomination and a clear deadline. Participants filmed themselves pouring cold water over their heads, shared the clip online and invited friends to join or donate. The humorous videos attracted attention while introducing a serious illness to people who might not otherwise have heard about it.

Its success also raised questions. Some viewers remembered the entertainment but not the cause, and public pressure may have encouraged people to participate without understanding the charity. Online campaigns can disappear quickly once a new trend arrives. A strong fundraiser therefore needs reliable information, transparent donation arrangements and a way to keep supporters involved after the videos stop circulating.

Students could design other digital activities such as a sponsored skills challenge, an online performance or a team quiz. The activity should be safe, easy to explain and suitable for people with different abilities. Popularity matters, but the group should also judge whether the idea raises useful awareness, protects participants and directs support to a trustworthy organisation.

context.title: Hong Kong Observatory signals: Discussion Context
body: Hong Kong uses a range of signals to warn the public about typhoons, heavy rain, thunderstorms and other dangerous conditions. The system gives schools, families and businesses a shared reference point for making safety decisions. Clear warnings can reduce travel during severe weather and allow emergency services to prepare before conditions become worse.

However, the same signal may affect districts differently. A warning can close schools even when the weather near some campuses appears calm, while transport disruption and childcare problems create difficulties for working families. Businesses also need to decide when staff should leave, and members of the public may misunderstand what each signal actually requires them to do.

Improvements could include more district-specific information, clearer mobile alerts and practical advice linked to each warning. Any change must remain simple enough to understand quickly and must not encourage people to ignore territory-wide risks. The Observatory, schools, employers and transport operators should communicate consistently so that safety messages do not compete with one another.

context.title: EQ: Discussion Context
body: Emotional intelligence, often called EQ, involves recognising feelings, managing reactions and responding appropriately to other people. Students may experience anxiety about examinations, disagreements with friends, family expectations or uncertainty about the future. If they cannot discuss these emotions or recover from setbacks, concentration and relationships may suffer even when their academic ability is strong.

A high EQ does not replace knowledge or reasoning, but it can help people cooperate, make decisions under pressure and ask for support. These skills develop through experience rather than a single lesson. Group work, sport, creative activities and family conversations can all give young people opportunities to listen, negotiate and understand different points of view.

Schools could teach students how to name emotions, handle conflict and recognise when professional help is needed. Peer-support programmes and trained counsellors may make help easier to seek. Activities should not force students to reveal private experiences in public. The aim is to build a respectful environment in which emotional skills are practised alongside academic learning.

context.title: Libraries: Discussion Context
body: Public libraries compete with smartphones, streaming services and the large amount of free information available online. Teenagers may still value quiet study space, reliable internet access and books they cannot afford to buy. Yet some see libraries as places with strict rules, outdated collections and few reasons to visit once schoolwork is finished.

Modern libraries can offer more than shelves of printed books. Digital lending, media-making equipment, reading clubs and talks with writers can connect traditional services with young people’s interests. Flexible seating and group areas may also help students who have little study space at home. These changes require funding, staff training and careful management of noise.

New activities should support the library’s educational purpose rather than turn it into another shopping centre. Teenagers could help choose events and recommend materials, while librarians could teach how to judge whether online information is trustworthy. A successful library would provide both quiet and collaborative zones and remain accessible to people who do not own expensive devices.

context.title: Road Safety: Discussion Context
body: Road accidents in Hong Kong have fallen over time as vehicles, roads and public education have improved. Seat belts, airbags, better lighting and safer junctions reduce some risks, while enforcement discourages dangerous driving. Technology can also warn drivers when they leave a lane or approach an obstacle.

Safety equipment cannot prevent every collision. Speeding, drink-driving, mobile-phone use and tiredness still depend on human choices. Pedestrians may cross between vehicles or look at screens instead of traffic, and cyclists can be vulnerable when roads do not provide enough space. Older people and children may need more time and clearer signals when crossing.

Reducing accidents requires drivers, passengers and pedestrians to share responsibility. Schools can teach practical road behaviour, the government can improve crossings and cycle routes, and police can target the most dangerous offences. Campaigns are most useful when they explain the consequences of risky behaviour and are supported by road design that makes the safer choice easier.

context.title: Keeping the Elderly Active: Discussion Context
body: Groups of older residents often gather in parks to sing, dance and play music. The activity is inexpensive, social and easy to join, so it can reduce loneliness and help participants remain physically and mentally active. Performers may also enjoy sharing songs that carry memories from earlier stages of their lives.

Outdoor performances can disturb nearby residents and other park users, especially when amplifiers are loud or several groups compete for space. Strict bans may reduce complaints, but they can also create conflict and remove an activity that many elderly people value. Building a costly performance venue will not help if it is inconvenient or difficult to book.

A balanced plan could set reasonable hours and sound limits, designate several performance areas and provide indoor alternatives during bad weather. Performers should help monitor noise, while officials should explain rules consistently. Community centres, underused sports facilities and sheltered public spaces could offer additional venues without excluding other users.

context.title: Legal age: Discussion Context
body: Hong Kong law sets different minimum ages for activities such as employment, driving, marriage and getting a tattoo. These limits are intended to protect young people and the public when a decision carries lasting consequences or requires mature judgement. Tattoo rules are especially strict because an unsafe procedure can cause infection and the result may be difficult to remove.

A single legal age cannot measure the maturity of every teenager. Some young people can manage responsibility earlier than others, while parental permission does not always remove health or safety risks. Different activities also involve different levels of danger, so it is reasonable for the limits not to be identical.

When reviewing an age limit, the government should consider evidence about harm, young people’s rights and whether the rule can be enforced. Education and access to trustworthy advice may work better than punishment alone. Any proposed change should explain why that age is suitable and what additional safeguards, supervision or consent would still be required.

context.title: Social Problems: Discussion Context
body: Some young people withdraw from face-to-face contact for long periods and spend most of their time alone at home. The causes can include anxiety, bullying, academic pressure, family conflict or fear of failure. Technology may make isolation easier to maintain, but using the internet is not itself proof that a person has a serious social problem.

Extended withdrawal can interrupt education, employment, sleep and physical health. Families may feel helpless if direct pressure leads to arguments or deeper avoidance. The young person may also lose confidence in ordinary activities, making it harder to return to school or reconnect with friends.

Support should begin with patient, non-judgemental contact and an effort to understand the individual’s circumstances. Families can seek advice from counsellors or health professionals, while schools can offer flexible return plans and a trusted adult to speak with. Small steps, such as regular routines and low-pressure activities, may be more effective than demanding an immediate return to normal life.

context.title: Boot camps: Discussion Context
body: Some parents send children to military-style boot camps because they believe modern family life has made young people dependent and unwilling to face difficulty. Campers may have to wake early, complete physical tasks, clean shared facilities and manage without domestic help. Supporters say the experience can teach discipline, teamwork and basic self-care.

A harsh programme may also humiliate children, create safety risks or confuse obedience with independence. Young people have different physical and emotional needs, and a short period of discomfort does not automatically change habits at home. Parents who solve every problem for their children may need to change their own behaviour as well.

Independence can be developed through ordinary responsibilities such as budgeting, cooking, planning travel, volunteering or joining a supervised outdoor programme. If a boot camp is considered, its staff, safety standards and methods should be checked carefully. The goal should be confidence and responsibility, not punishment or fear.

context.title: Food: Discussion Context
body: Food can influence energy, concentration and mood, although no single item guarantees that a person will feel happy. Meals containing protein, fruit, vegetables and whole grains may provide steadier energy than snacks high in sugar. Schools therefore have a reason to consider both nutrition and how appealing their menus are to students.

A menu offering only foods labelled healthy may be unpopular if choices are expensive, unfamiliar or badly prepared. Claims about mood-enhancing foods can also be exaggerated. Stress, sleep, exercise and relationships may affect emotions more strongly than one meal, and students with allergies or medical needs require suitable alternatives.

Schools could provide clear information, affordable balanced meals and smaller portions of less nutritious treats instead of imposing a complete ban. Students could taste-test new dishes and help improve presentation. The aim should be to make a healthy choice convenient and enjoyable while teaching students to evaluate health claims rather than follow fashionable advice.

context.title: Good teachers are the most important factor in educational success: Discussion Context
body: Good teachers can explain difficult ideas, notice when learners are confused and create a classroom where students are willing to participate. Their expectations and feedback may strongly influence confidence and progress. For students with limited support outside school, a skilled teacher can be especially important.

Educational success nevertheless depends on more than teaching. Students must practise, persist and take responsibility for their work. Family support, school resources, class size, health and prior knowledge also shape results. Even an excellent teacher cannot control every factor, while motivated learners sometimes succeed despite weak instruction.

A debate on this motion should first define both “good teachers” and “educational success”. One side may argue that teachers connect all other resources to the learner; the other may stress effort and circumstances beyond the classroom. The strongest conclusion will compare the relative influence of each factor rather than claiming that teachers either determine everything or make no difference.

context.title: The importance of smartphones in China: Discussion Context
body: Smartphones have changed how people in China communicate, pay for services, travel and obtain information. For many users, one device can replace a camera, wallet, map and computer. This convenience has helped mobile services grow quickly, but it also means that cost, data access and digital skills affect who receives the benefits.

A premium international brand may struggle when the economy slows and strong local competitors offer capable phones at lower prices. Fashion also changes: a device once treated as a status symbol may become less distinctive. Brand reputation, software, after-sales service and links with other products can still persuade some customers to pay more.

Future success will depend on whether new features solve real problems and whether prices match consumers’ expectations. The group should distinguish the importance of smartphones in general from the prospects of one company. It should also consider privacy, distraction, electronic waste and unequal access when judging whether wider smartphone use is entirely positive.

context.title: Online Games Day at school: Discussion Context
body: A study reported that teenagers who regularly played online games achieved slightly higher results in some school subjects. Many games require players to read instructions, solve puzzles, manage resources and cooperate with teammates. These skills could support learning, although the finding does not prove that gaming itself caused the better scores.

A school Online Games Day might include strategy tournaments, collaborative puzzles and student-designed educational games. Activities could interest students who do not usually join sports events and provide opportunities to discuss teamwork and digital citizenship. Organisers would still need suitable devices, a stable network and games that are appropriate for different ages.

Possible problems include excessive screen time, unfair access to equipment, online behaviour and competition becoming too intense. The school should set sensible time limits, provide non-digital breaks and avoid games that reward spending money. Success should be judged by participation and learning, not only by who wins.

context.title: Working Holidays: Discussion Context
body: A working holiday allows young adults to fund part of their travel by taking temporary jobs overseas. Advertisements may offer farm work, fruit picking or jobs on tourist boats. Participants can meet local people, improve language skills and learn to manage money and daily life away from home.

The experience can also involve long hours, basic accommodation, remote locations and work that is more physically demanding than expected. An attractive advertisement may not explain wages, insurance, transport or visa conditions clearly. Some students may be prepared for customer service work but not for operating equipment or living far from medical help.

Applicants should check employers, contracts and legal requirements before travelling. They also need emergency savings, health cover and a realistic plan for communication with family. Other suitable jobs might include hospitality, childcare or event support, depending on skills and local rules. A successful working holiday combines travel with safe, lawful employment rather than treating any overseas job as an adventure.

context.title: Giving blood: Discussion Context
body: Hong Kong hospitals need a reliable supply of donated blood for surgery, emergencies and the treatment of serious illness. Young first-time donors can help meet present needs and may continue donating as adults. A school collection can also show students how one voluntary action supports people they may never meet.

Some students are unable to donate because of age, health or eligibility rules, while others are anxious about needles, pain or feeling unwell. Pressure from classmates could make a voluntary event uncomfortable. Organisers therefore need accurate screening information, trained medical staff, privacy and a clear message that declining is acceptable.

The school could hold the event in a quiet, accessible hall at a time that does not conflict with examinations or strenuous activities. Talks from medical staff, donor stories and opportunities to ask questions may reduce fear. Students who cannot give blood could help with publicity or logistics, allowing the campaign to encourage participation without treating donation as compulsory.

context.title: Tourists: Discussion Context
body: A travel-book cover has to attract attention while giving readers an honest idea of Hong Kong. Harbour views and dense city streets show energy and an international skyline, while temples, country parks and geological landscapes reveal heritage and natural space that some visitors may not expect.

A familiar skyline is easy to recognise, but it can repeat an image already used by many travel guides. A less familiar photograph may create curiosity yet fail to communicate the city immediately. The choice also depends on the intended readers and whether the book focuses on culture, outdoor travel, architecture or a general introduction.

The group should compare what each image includes and what it leaves out. A strong cover needs visual impact, a clear connection with the book and enough originality to stand out. If one photograph cannot represent the city’s contrasts, the designer might use a carefully balanced composition, provided it remains simple and does not mislead visitors.

context.title: More bus lanes are needed in Hong Kong: Discussion Context
body: Buses carry a large share of Hong Kong passengers, but their journeys can become slow and unreliable in heavy traffic. Supporters of more bus lanes argue that giving priority to vehicles carrying many people would shorten travel times, make timetables more dependable and encourage drivers to leave private cars at home.

Opponents point out that road space is limited. Removing a general traffic lane could worsen congestion for taxis, delivery vehicles and people who must drive for work. A bus lane that is poorly located or active all day may remain underused at quieter times and move pollution rather than reduce it.

Possible compromises include peak-hour lanes, better enforcement, traffic-signal priority and regular reviews of passenger numbers. Other solutions could involve congestion charges, improved interchange between buses and rail, and better information for passengers. The group should judge proposals by how many people benefit, their effect on journey times and whether they reduce total traffic.

context.title: Discrimination against older people: Discussion Context
body: Some capable employees are required to leave work at a fixed retirement age even when they wish to continue. Older workers may offer experience, reliability and knowledge that can be passed to younger colleagues. Continuing employment can also provide income, routine and social contact as people live longer.

Employers may worry about health, training costs or whether promotion opportunities for younger staff will be reduced. Yet decisions based only on age can ignore large differences between individuals. Keeping everyone in the same role indefinitely may not be suitable, but automatically excluding applicants over a certain age is also unfair.

Reducing discrimination could involve flexible hours, retraining, phased retirement and recruitment based on ability rather than stereotypes. Government guidance and legal protection may help, but workplaces also need practical ways to review performance and adapt duties. The aim should be genuine choice: older people should neither be forced out of suitable work nor pressured to continue when they prefer to retire.

context.title: Keeping Hong Kong's Streets Clean: Discussion Context
body: An elderly cleaner on a modest wage was fined after pouring waste water onto a street. Her employer later offered to pay the penalty. The case led to debate about whether a standard fine treats everyone equally when the same amount creates very different hardship for people with different incomes.

Fines can communicate that littering and pollution are unacceptable, and simple fixed penalties are easy to understand. However, punishment may appear unfair when rules are unclear, enforcement is inconsistent or an offence happens during work. Very high penalties can create financial distress without changing the behaviour that caused the problem.

Clean streets also depend on convenient bins, public education, responsible employers and consistent enforcement. Alternatives such as warnings, community service or income-related penalties could be considered, but each may be harder to administer. A fair system should distinguish deliberate dumping from minor mistakes while still requiring individuals and companies to prevent waste from entering public spaces.

context.title: Planning a Safe Night Hike and Camp
body: A group of students is considering a night hike and overnight camp on a Hong Kong mountain to mark graduation. Walking after dark can feel adventurous, offer cooler temperatures and give hikers a chance to see the city lights or sunrise. Sharing the challenge may also strengthen friendships at the end of school.

Night travel makes familiar risks harder to manage. Paths can be difficult to follow, weather can change, and tired hikers may fall or become separated. Each participant needs suitable shoes, water, warm and waterproof clothing, a charged torch and emergency contact arrangements. Heavy bags and unnecessary equipment can make the route more difficult.

The group should choose a route that matches everyone’s experience, check official weather and trail information, and tell a responsible person about the plan. Camping must be allowed at the chosen site, and students should carry out all rubbish. A clear meeting system and a willingness to cancel in unsafe conditions are more important than reaching the summit on schedule.
